## Score Descriptions:

### Vulnerability:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Vulnerability on the Northeast Shelf for Bluefish"
#| label: fig-vuln
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_vulnerability_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean Vulnerability for Bluefish was **Low** (3.11 +/- 0.69) due to Low Sensitivity scores (@fig-sum-tab). Vulnerability was Moderate along Georges Bank and south of Cape Cod but Low throughout the rest of their range (@fig-vuln). Vulnerability remained Low when only factors important to species distributions were used to calculate Exposure (@fig-sum-tab).

In the previous Assessment, Bluefish also received a Low Vulnerability score [@hare2016vulnerability].

### Climate Exposure:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_exposure_map_all", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result

```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Exposure on the Northeast Shelf for Bluefish"
#| label: fig-exp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_exposure_map_all", ext)))
```

Mean Exposure was **High** (3.11 +/- 0.69) (@fig-sum-tab). Bluefish exposure was Very High along Georges Bank and south of Cape Cod, and Low off the coast of Chesapeake Bay (@fig-exp). These patterns were driven by high exposure to changes in sea surface temperature, salinity, and pH (@fig-fact-exp). In the previous Assessment, Bluefish also received a High Exposure score due to high exposure to sea surface temperature and ocean acidification [@hare2016vulnerability].

#### Exposure from Significant Variables

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_exposure_map_timeseries_imp", ext))

```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Exposure and Monthly Variability Based on Factors critical to Bluefish distributions"
#| label: fig-exp-imp
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/total_exposure_map_timeseries_imp", ext)))
```

Sea surface temperature, surface salinity, and small zooplankton biomass were the major drivers of bluefish distribution (@fig-sum-tab). While adult bluefish are piscivores, larvae are dependent on copepod prey [@Shepherd2006]. Bluefish juveniles utilize estuary habitats, and temperature is a major driver of migration timing [@Smith1994]. When only these important factors were used in the exposure calculation, exposure was Moderate due to changes in zooplankton biomass exposure (@fig-exp-imp).

### Biological Sensitivity:

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Define the path to the potential image
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
img_path <- here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/sensitivity_map", ext))

# Store the TRUE/FALSE result 
has_figure <- file.exists(img_path)
```

```{r,echo=FALSE, fig.align='center'}
#| lightbox: true
#| eval: !expr has_figure
#| fig-cap: "Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf"
#| label: fig-sens
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-align: "center"
#| fig-pos: "H"
ext <- ifelse(knitr::is_latex_output(), ".pdf", ".png")
knitr::include_graphics(here::here(paste0("figures/Bluefish/sensitivity_map", ext)))
```

Bluefish received a **Low** sensitivity score, with a certainty of 69% (@fig-sum-tab). The only attribute that received a score greater than 2.5 was Juvenile Habitat Requirements (4) (@fig-sum-tab). Bluefish rely entirely on salt marshes and submerged aquatic vegetation as juveniles; both habitats are considered highly vulnerable to future climate change [@guyant2022northeast].

Bluefish also received a Low sensitivity score in the 2016 Assessment. Similar to our results, Early Life History Requirements was the only attribute to score above 2.5 [@hare2016vulnerability].

### Directional Effect:

Bluefish are expected to be **neutrally** impacted by climate change. Expert certainty was 95%. Distributions are shifting north and east and warming temperatures may expand the spawning season [@Tyrell2022]. However, there is a concern that seasonal mismatches may occur if juveniles arrive in estuaries before their prey, which may impact recruitment [@Taylor2006]. In the original Assessment, bluefish were predicted to be positively impacted by climate change due to expanding distributions and spawning seasons [@hare2016vulnerability].

## Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution

There has been a documented shift in bluefish distribution, spawning, habitat use in the Mediterranean [@Sabates2012] [@VillegasHernandez2015]. Bluefish distributions in the Northwest Atlantic seem to be shifting north and east [@Tyrell2022]. Increasing fall sea surface temperatures may extend spawning season further into the calendar year [@Tyrell2022]. If warming alters spawning phenology, there are concerns that juveniles may arrive in estuaries before their prey. Seasonal mismatches have been shown to impact growth, body condition, and reproductive success [@Taylor2006]. Changing distributions of prey species as a result of climate change may alter interactions between bluefish and their prey [@Whitfield2026].

## Life History Synopsis

Bluefish inhabit temperate and tropical surface waters in the North Atlantic from Maine to the Atlantic coast of Florida [@Shepherd2006]. Bluefish in the North Atlantic are a single, migratory stock with two discrete spawning periods. The first occurs during March-May near the edge of the continental shelf of the South-Atlantic Bight. The second occurs between June and August in the Mid-Atlantic Bight [@Shepherd2006]. Eggs hatch after 46-48 hours at 18 - 22.2°C to pelagic larvae [@Deuel1966]. Larvae spawned in the South Atlantic (spring-spawned cohort) are subject to advection north via the Gulf Stream and inshore via warm core rings. Eggs in the southern part of the Mid-Atlantic Bight may be advected south and offshore [@Shepherd2006]. Transport of larvae and/or juveniles across the shelf- slope region may be aided by wind-driven surface flow [@Hare1996]. @Sherman1984 note that wide distribution of bluefish larvae over the shelf reduces their vulnerability to the predator field and environmental perturbation. Larvae prey on copepods [@Shepherd2006]. Peak abundance of larval bluefish in Southern New England and the Mid-Atlantic Bight coincided with zooplankton production [@Sherman1984]. Changes in prey availability and distribution can impact bluefish condition and reproductive success [@Taylor2006]. Juvenile bluefish inhabit estuaries, bays, and coastal oceans with sand, oyster beds, and submerged aquatic vegetation habitats [@McBride1991]. Juveniles enter estuaries when temperatures are greater than 13-15°C and leave when temperatures fall below 10-12°C [@Smith1994]. Juvenile migration into estuarine habitats appears tied to a shift in eating other fish. In estuaries, adults and juveniles eat whatever taxa are locally abundant (fish, crustaceans, shrimp, and polychaetes). In ocean habitats, young-of-the-year bluefish switch to piscivory predation with increasing size, similar to estuarine habitats [@Marks1996]. Bluefish are opportunistic foragers, and the composition of adult bluefish diet depends largely on the available prey, but they consume similar prey items as juvenile bluefish [@Shepherd2006]. Bluefish have long been recognized as a notable predator of forage fish [@Tyrell2022]. Adult bluefish conduct seasonal migrations following warmer waters, overwintering in the south and moving north in the spring and summer [@Shepherd2006]. Migrations may be cued by photoperiod as well, and have been observed to shift northward in warm years [@Nye2009]. Shortfin mako sharks are identified as a major predator of bluefish and may consume more individuals than removed by the fishery [@Wood2009]. Most bluefish are mature by age 2, with approximately half maturing by age 1 [@NEFSC2015_bluefish]. The maximum age for bluefish in the North Atlantic is 12 years [@Salerno2001]. In the Northwest Atlantic, bluefish are managed by the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council and Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission. The last stock assessment occurred in 2025, where bluefish were found to not be overfished nor is overfishing occurring [@NEFSC2025_bluefish].
